lesson.title: When Authority Speaks: The Psychology of Obedience
lesson.summary: Obedience is behavior change produced by a direct command from a perceived authority figure, and Stanley Milgram's controversial experiments in the early 1960s remain the most influential, and most ethically debated, demonstration of just how far ordinary people will go in following orders that conflict with their own conscience.
lesson.body:
Obedience is closely related to conformity, since both involve social norms and social influence shaping behavior, but the two are worth distinguishing carefully. Conformity typically involves matching the implicit example set by peers, with no one directly telling the person what to do. Obedience specifically involves a clear, direct command from someone perceived to hold legitimate authority, and it depends heavily on the power or status differential between the person giving the order and the person receiving it.

The most famous research on obedience was conducted by Stanley Milgram at Yale University in the early 1960s. In the best known version of his experiments, a participant was assigned the role of "teacher" and instructed by an experimenter, who wore a lab coat and projected calm authority, to deliver increasingly strong electric shocks to a "learner" in another room each time the learner answered a memory question incorrectly. In reality, the shocks were never actually administered and the learner was a confederate, but participants believed the situation was completely real, including the learner's recorded protests, complaints of pain, and eventual ominous silence as the shock levels climbed toward a labeled maximum of 450 volts. In this baseline version of the study, a widely cited figure of roughly two thirds of participants, about sixty five percent, continued administering shocks all the way to the maximum level, despite frequently showing visible signs of significant distress while doing so.

Milgram also ran a number of variations that revealed obedience was far from fixed. It was highly sensitive to the situation. Obedience dropped sharply when the teacher was placed in the same room as the learner, or especially when required to physically hold the learner's hand onto the shock plate, when the experimenter gave orders by telephone from another room rather than in person, and when the participant saw other "teachers," actually confederates, refuse to continue. To help explain why so many otherwise ordinary participants complied, Milgram proposed the idea of an agentic state, a psychological shift in which a person stops seeing themselves as personally responsible for their actions and instead experiences themselves as merely an instrument carrying out another person's will, which can make it much easier to continue an act that would otherwise feel unconscionable.

Milgram's obedience studies raised major ethical concerns that have had a lasting impact on the field. Participants were deceived about the true nature of the study, experienced genuine and sometimes severe psychological distress believing they had harmed another person, and were not given the kind of full informed consent or clear freedom to withdraw that modern research standards require. These concerns are widely credited as one of the key catalysts for the development of formal research ethics oversight in psychology, including institutional review boards that must approve human research in advance and revised ethical codes from professional organizations such as the American Psychological Association, which now require protections such as thorough debriefing, minimizing unnecessary harm, and a clearly communicated right to withdraw at any time. A study very much like Milgram's original design could not be conducted today without substantial modification for exactly these reasons.
